NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament :: Format :: Venues :: chunk_0015
In the men's tournament, all sites are nominally neutral; teams are prohibited from playing tournament games on their home courts during the first, second, and regional rounds. Under NCAA rules, any court on which a team hosts more than three regular-season games (not including preseason or conference tournament games) is considered a "home court".[[13]](#cite_note-NCAABracketPrinciples-15) For the First Four and the Final Four, the home court prohibition does not apply because only one venue hosts these rounds. The First Four is regularly hosted by the [Dayton Flyers](/wiki/Dayton_Flyers_men%27s_basketball "Dayton Flyers men's basketball"); as such, the team competed on their home court in [2015](/wiki/2015_NCAA_Division_I_men%27s_basketball_tournament "2015 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament").[[15]](#cite_note-17) Because the Final Four is hosted at indoor football stadiums, it is unlikely that a team will play on their home court in the future. The last time this was possible was in [1996](/wiki/1996_NCAA_Division_I_men%27s_basketball_tournament "1996 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament") when the [Continental Airlines Arena](/wiki/Continental_Airlines_Arena "Continental Airlines Arena"), home court of [Seton Hall](/wiki/Seton_Hall_Pirates_men%27s_basketball "Seton Hall Pirates men's basketball"), hosted.

For the first and second rounds, eight venues host games, four on each day of the round. Each venue hosts two sets of four teams, referred to as "pods." To limit travel, teams are placed in pods closer to their home unless seeding rules would prevent it. Because each pod includes a top 4 seed, the highest ranked teams normally get the closest sites.

The possible pods by seeding are:

* Pod A: 1 v. 16 and 8 v. 9
* Pod B: 2 v. 15 and 7 v. 10
* Pod C: 3 v. 14 and 6 v. 11
* Pod D: 4 v. 13 and 5 v. 12

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/PC%27s_Limited_Turbo_PC.jpg/250px-PC%27s_Limited_Turbo_PC.jpg)](/wiki/File:PC%27s_Limited_Turbo_PC.jpg)

The first PC model, manufactured by Dell (known as PC's Limited at the time), the Turbo PC

[Michael Dell](/wiki/Michael_Dell "Michael Dell") founded Dell Computer Corporation, doing business as PC's Limited, in 1984. Dell was a student at the [University of Texas at Austin](/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin"),[[15]](#cite_note-15) and operated the business from his off-campus dormitory room at [Dobie Center](/wiki/Dobie_Center "Dobie Center").[[16]](#cite_note-16) The start-up aimed to sell [IBM PC compatible](/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible") computers built from stock components. Michael Dell started trading in the belief that, by selling personal computer systems directly to customers, PC's Limited could better understand customers' needs and provide the most effective computing services to meet those needs.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Dell dropped out of college upon completion of his freshman year at the University of Texas in order to focus full-time on his fledgling business, after getting about $1,000 in expansion-capital from his family.[[18]](#cite_note-delltimeline-18) As of April 2021, Dell's net worth was estimated to be over $50 billion (equivalent to $56,940,000,000 in 2024).[[19]](#cite_note-19)

In 1985, PC's Limited launched its first computer, the "Turbo PC", priced at US$795 (equivalent to $1,963 in 2024).[[20]](#cite_note-20) The Turbo PC featured an Intel 8088-compatible processor with a maximum speed of 8 MHz.[[21]](#cite_note-21) At that time PC's Limited was considered one of many [white box](/wiki/White_box_(computer_hardware) "White box (computer hardware)") vendors, although by 1986 [Hughes Aircraft](/wiki/Hughes_Aircraft "Hughes Aircraft") was evaluating its products for corporate use af

On August 13, 2018, Anthony signed a one-year, $2.4 million veterans minimum contract with the [Houston Rockets](/wiki/Houston_Rockets "Houston Rockets") coached by his former Knicks coach, [Mike D'Antoni](/wiki/Mike_D%27Antoni "Mike D'Antoni").[[200]](#cite_note-200)[[201]](#cite_note-201)[[202]](#cite_note-stein_11152018-202) On November 15, Rockets general manager [Daryl Morey](/wiki/Daryl_Morey "Daryl Morey") announced that the team was "parting ways" with Anthony, but had not released him. He played ten games for Houston, starting twice, but he was held out of the last three for what the club called an unspecified "illness."[[202]](#cite_note-stein_11152018-202) During that absence, much of his playing time went to rookie [Gary Clark](/wiki/Gary_Clark_(basketball) "Gary Clark (basketball)").[[203]](#cite_note-203) Houston had started the season losing seven of their first 11 games. Morey said that Anthony "accepted every role" asked by D'Antoni, but that the "fit we envisioned when Carmelo chose to sign with the Rockets has not materialized; therefore we thought it was best to move on as any other outcome would have been unfair to him." D'Antoni stated that he "didn't ever want to disrespect [Anthony] and his career. He's going in the Hall of Fame."[[202]](#cite_note-stein_11152018-202)

On January 22, 2019, the Rockets traded Anthony, the draft rights to [Jon Diebler](/wiki/Jon_Diebler "Jon Diebler"), and undisclosed cash considerations to the [Chicago Bulls](/wiki/Chicago_Bulls "Chicago Bulls") in exchange for the draft rights to [Tadija Dragićević](/wiki/Tadija_Dragi%C4%87evi%C4%87 "Tadija Dragićević").[[204]](#cite_note-204) This trade allowed the Rockets to alleviate luxury-tax penalties up to $2.6 million.[[205]](#cite_note-205) On February 1, he was waived by the Bulls.[[206]](#cite_note-206)

Nutter was born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and grew up in [West Philadelphia](/wiki/West_Philadelphia "West Philadelphia"). Raised [Catholic](/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church"), he attended elementary school at Transfiguration of Our Lord Catholic Elementary School and later [St. Joseph's Preparatory School](/wiki/St._Joseph%27s_Preparatory_School "St. Joseph's Preparatory School") in [North Philadelphia](/wiki/North_Philadelphia "North Philadelphia") where he was known affectionately as "Big Nut".[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) He graduated from [The Wharton School](/wiki/Wharton_School "Wharton School") at the [University of Pennsylvania](/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania") in 1979 with a degree in business.[[7]](#cite_note-7) During his [sophomore year](/wiki/Sophomore "Sophomore") in college, he started working as a [DJ](/wiki/Disc_jockey "Disc jockey") at Club Impulse in Philadelphia, where he was known as Mix Master Mike.[[8]](#cite_note-8) After graduating from college, Nutter began to work at [Xerox](/wiki/Xerox "Xerox"), and then at an [investment banking](/wiki/Investment_banking "Investment banking") firm. While in office, Nutter occasionally worked as DJ and a singer.

Nutter, then-leader of the 52nd ward of Philadelphia, initially challenged [Democratic](/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") incumbent [Ann Land](/wiki/Ann_Land "Ann Land") for a seat on the [Philadelphia City Council](/wiki/Philadelphia_City_Council "Philadelphia City Council") in 1987.[[9]](#cite_note-LandObit-9) He was unsuccessful in his initial bid but defeated Land, four years later.[[9]](#cite_note-LandObit-9)

In February 2003, Nutter was elected chairman of the [Pennsylvania Convention Center Authority Board](/wiki/Pennsylvania_Convention_Center "Pennsylvania Convention Center").[[10]](#cite_note-10)

The current [NFL schedule](/wiki/NFL_regular_season#Scheduling_formula "NFL regular season") begins on the weekend immediately after [Labor Day](/wiki/Labor_Day "Labor Day") (the first Monday in September). That weekend is the first of an 18-week [regular season](/wiki/NFL_regular_season "NFL regular season"), followed by three weeks of [playoff games](/wiki/NFL_playoffs "NFL playoffs") and one week for the [Pro Bowl](/wiki/Pro_Bowl "Pro Bowl"). The Super Bowl is contested the week after the Pro Bowl. This schedule has been in effect since an 18th week and 17th regular season game were added to the NFL schedule for the 2021 season, with [Super Bowl LVI](/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVI "Super Bowl LVI") on February 13, 2022, the first to be played under this format.

Economy of Luxembourg :: Energy :: chunk_0012
Main article: [Energy in Luxembourg](/wiki/Energy_in_Luxembourg "Energy in Luxembourg")

In 1978, Luxembourg tried to build a 1,200 [MW](/wiki/Watt#Megawatt "Watt") nuclear reactor but dropped the plans after threats of major protests.[[49]](#cite_note-49)
Luxembourg uses imported oil and natural gas for the majority of its energy generation.[[50]](#cite_note-50) The [Cattenom Nuclear Power Plant](/wiki/Cattenom_Nuclear_Power_Plant "Cattenom Nuclear Power Plant") across the border in France's [Grand Est](/wiki/Grand_Est "Grand Est") region produces more electricity than the entire country of Luxembourg consumes, however, due to the strength of the [anti-nuclear movement](/wiki/Anti-nuclear_movement "Anti-nuclear movement") in Luxembourg, electricity exports directly from France to Luxembourg are hampered by lack of infrastructure.
